title: The Interventionist Future of the DSA
author: Philip Cunliffe
content:
![The Interventionist Future of the
DSA](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/07/AP26199828668861.jpg)

Donald Trump campaigned on ending America's "forever wars" in the Middle East.
In office, however, he opened up a new front in those conflicts by striking
Iran. However the current conflict turns out, Trump's trajectory bears a
striking resemblance to that of Barack Obama. Like Trump, Obama campaigned
against America's involvement in the Middle East. Yet despite Obama's soaring
rhetoric and promise of a "pivot to Asia," he proved unable to extricate the
United States from the region. To the contrary, he bombed Libya in 2011 and
Syria in 2014, with effects arguably as catastrophic as those of Bush's
intervention against Saddam Hussein. The stewardship of America's "forever
wars" thus passed from the neoconservatives of the Bush White House to the
liberal humanitarians of the Obama era and then to the national populists
under Trump.

Which will be the next faction to take up the baton? Currently, the strongest
candidates for the role are the members of the Democratic coalition affiliated
with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Like Obama and Trump before
them, this new crop of populists is gaining traction as vocal critics of US
foreign policy. Like Trump when he was in the opposition, these opponents now
criticize the president from the political position that he abandoned. For
instance, Abdul el Sayed, a DSA
[_ally_](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/06/dsa-progressives-wisconsin-
michigan-primaries-00986944?ref=compactmag.com) currently running to be
Michigan's Democratic candidate for the Senate, is standing on a de facto
America First platform of the left, attacking the Trump administration for
embroiling itself in a regional war that serves Israeli interests more than US
ones.
